{{Elections in Oklahoma}}
The '''2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Oklahoma''' were held on November 8, 2022, to elect the five [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representatives]] from the [[U.S. state|state]] of [[Oklahoma]], one from each of the state's five [[Oklahoma's congressional districts|congressional districts]]. The [[primary elections]] for the [[Republican Party of Oklahoma|Republican]]. [[Democratic Party of Oklahoma|Democratic]], and [[Libertarian Party of Oklahoma|Libertarian]] parties' nominations took place on June 28, 2022.<ref name="2022 Election Dates & Deadlines">{{cite web |title=2022 Statutory Election Dates and Deadlines |url=https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/dates-and-deadlines/2022-statutory-dates-deadlines.pdf |website=oklahoma.gov |publisher=Oklahoma State Election Board |access-date=October 13, 2021 |archive-date=April 25, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220425080130/https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/dates-and-deadlines/2022-statutory-dates-deadlines.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The 2022 election cycle was the first election following [[Redistricting in the United States|redistricting]] in 2020–21. Redistricting in Oklahoma was postponed to a special legislative session, because of the [[2020 United States census]] data's release being delayed.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Savage |first1=Tres |title=Special session 'the only option we have' on redistricting |url=https://nondoc.com/2021/04/01/fall-special-session-coming-for-redistricting/ |website=Nondoc |date=April 2021 |publisher=NonDoc Media |access-date=April 2, 2021}}</ref> New congressional districts were signed into law based on data from the [[2020 United States census]] on November 22, 2021.<ref>{{cite web |title=Governor Kevin Stitt Signs Six Redistricting Bills into Law |url=https://oklahoma.gov/governor/newsroom/newsroom/2021/november/governor-kevin-stitt-signs-six-redistricting-bills-into-law.html |website=oklahoma.gov |publisher=Office of Governor J. {{see also|Oklahoma's 2nd congressional district}}
The incumbent was Republican [[Markwayne Mullin]], who was re-elected with 75% of the vote in [[2020 United States House of Representatives elections in Oklahoma|2020]].<ref name="Nov3,2020Results" /> On February 26, 2022, Mullin announced his retirement and ran for U.S. Senate.<ref name=Mullin>{{cite news |last1=Morris |first1=Callie |title=Rep. Markwayne Mullin announces run for Senate |url= https://ktul.com/news/local/markwayne-mullin-announces-run-for-us-senate |publisher=KTUL News |date=February 26, 2022 |access-date=February 26, 2022}}</ref> Since only one candidate filed for the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]]'s nomination there was no Democratic primary.

===Republican primary===
The 14 candidate Republican primary for Oklahoma's 2nd Congressional district is the largest Republican primary since 1936 when 15 Republican candidate ran for [[Oklahoma Corporation Commission|Oklahoma Corporate Commissioner]] and the largest primary in the state since the 24-candidate 1954 Democratic primary for [[Oklahoma Secretary of State]].<ref name="TW-CD2-12June2022">{{cite news |last1=Krehbiel |first1=Randy |title=Huge field turns CD 2 primary into a fight for survival |url=https://tulsaworld.com/news/state-and-regional/govt-and-politics/huge-field-turns-cd-2-primary-into-a-fight-for-survival/article_930bac66-e769-11ec-b4c1-a32a3b527518.html |access-date=June 12, 2022 |publisher=Tulsa World |date=June 12, 2022}}</ref>

Oklahoma's 2nd congressional district has been noted for drawing several tribal citizens to the race. After the ''[[McGirt v. Oklahoma]]'' decision there has been renewed interest in issues related to tribal sovereignty.<ref name="USHouse-NondocSummary" /> [[Guy Barker (politician)|Guy Barker]] is the secretary-treasurer of the [[Quapaw|Quapaw Nation]] and [[Wes Nofire]] is a [[Cherokee Nation]] tribal councilor.  [[Josh Brecheen]], [[Avery Frix]] and [[Dustin Roberts]] are members of the [[Choctaw Nation]] and Johnny Teehee is a member of the [[Cherokee Nation]].<ref name="USHouse-NondocSummary" />

At least one candidate, [[John R. Bennett]], called for the disestablishment of the [[Muscogee Nation]] in Oklahoma. The [[Five Civilized Tribes|Inter-Tribal Council of the Five Tribes]] denounced Bennett's candidacy in response to his calls for disestablishment.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harper |first1=Braden |title=Congressional candidate makes controversial statement on MCN |url=https://www.mvskokemedia.com/congressional-candidate-takes-controversial-state-on-mcn/ |access-date=May 9, 2022 |publisher=Mvskoke Media |date=April 28, 2022}}</ref>
